content.text: Opening a new database connection incurs a 30 ms overhead for the Ledger service due to the necessity of a TLS handshake and an authentication round trip.

content.text: A connection pool maintains a set of open connections, allowing requests to borrow them and bypass the connection establishment cost.

content.text: The pool limits the total number of connections the service can hold, safeguarding the database from potential overload during traffic spikes.

content.text: Connection pooling significantly reduces latency and protects the database from traffic spikes by reusing existing connections and limiting their total count.

ai.stableNodeKey: Running a shared connection pool › Why pool connections § text#3

content.text: Each Ledger instance runs a pool of at most 20 connections.¹ The database accepts 400 connections in total, and 40 of those are reserved for migrations and administrators.² That leaves room for 18 instances at full size, so the autoscaler is capped at 18 instances.³ Raising the pool size only helps while requests are waiting for a connection; once the database CPU is saturated, more connections make every query slower.⁴ A pool sized for peak traffic also holds idle connections at night, which costs memory on the database but nothing else.⁵
A request waits at most 2 seconds to borrow a connection before it fails with
POOL_EXHAUSTED
.⁶ The wait limit is deliberately shorter than the 5-second request deadline, so the caller still has time to return a clear error.⁷ Each query also has a statement timeout of 3 seconds, set with
SET statement_timeout = '3s'

when the connection is opened.⁸ The statement timeout does not apply to migrations, which run on their own reserved connections without a limit.⁹ A long transaction holds its connection for its whole duration, so the team keeps transactions under 500 ms.¹⁰
Before lending a connection that has been idle for more than 60 seconds, the pool runs
SELECT 1

to check that it still works.¹¹ A connection that fails the check is closed and replaced, and the request gets a fresh one.¹² During a database failover, every open connection breaks at once, so the pool is drained and refilled from the new primary.¹³ Refilling is limited to 5 new connections per second per instance, so that 18 instances reconnecting together don't overload the new primary.¹⁴ Until the pool is refilled, requests may see
POOL_EXHAUSTED
errors for up to about 4 seconds.¹⁵

A connection that stays borrowed for more than 10 seconds is logged as a possible leak, together with the stack trace of the code that borrowed it.¹⁶ The pool does not take a leaked connection back by force, because the code holding it may still be using it.¹⁷ Most leaks the team has found came from error paths that returned early without releasing the connection.¹⁸ Leak warnings are reviewed every week, and a leak that comes back gets a ticket for the team that owns the code.¹⁹

The pool exports three gauges: connections in use, idle connections, and requests waiting to borrow.²⁰ An alert pages the on-call engineer when requests have been waiting for more than 30 seconds in a row.²¹ A sustained queue usually means slow queries rather than a pool that is too small, so the runbook starts with the slowest statements, not with the pool size.²² The idle gauge drops to zero during a failover and recovers as the pool refills, which makes it a quick way to confirm that a failover has finished.²³

content.text:
¹ Each Ledger instance has a maximum of 20 connections.
 ² 40 connections are reserved for migrations and administrators, out of a total of 400.
 ³ The autoscaler is capped at 18 instances because 360 connections (400-40) divided by 20 connections per instance equals 18 instances.
 ⁴ Increasing pool size is only beneficial when requests are waiting for connections; it can worsen performance if the database CPU is already saturated.
 ⁵ Sizing the pool for peak traffic means idle connections consume database memory during off-peak hours.
 ⁶ Requests time out after 2 seconds if a connection isn't available.
 ⁷ This timeout is shorter than the 5-second request deadline to allow for proper error handling.
 ⁸ Queries have a 3-second statement timeout set upon connection.
 ⁹ Migrations are exempt from the statement timeout and use reserved connections.
 ¹⁰ Transactions are kept under 500 ms to prevent long-held connections.
 ¹¹ Connections idle for over 60 seconds are validated with
SELECT 1

before reuse.
 ¹² Failed connection checks result in closure, replacement, and a fresh connection for the request.
 ¹³ Database failover causes all open connections to break, leading to pool draining and refilling from the new primary.
 ¹⁴ Refilling is rate-limited to 5 new connections per second per instance to prevent overloading the new primary during mass reconnection.
 ¹⁵
POOL_EXHAUSTED

errors may occur for up to 4 seconds during pool refilling after a failover.
 ¹⁶ Connections borrowed for over 10 seconds are logged as potential leaks with their stack trace.
 ¹⁷ The pool does not forcibly reclaim leaked connections to avoid disrupting ongoing operations.
 ¹⁸ Most leaks are traced to error paths that fail to release connections.
 ¹⁹ Leak warnings are reviewed weekly, and recurring leaks lead to tickets for the owning team.
 ²⁰ The pool exposes metrics for connections in use, idle connections, and waiting requests.
 ²¹ An alert is triggered if requests wait for connections for more than 30 consecutive seconds.
 ²² A persistent queue typically indicates slow queries, not an undersized pool; the runbook prioritizes optimizing slow statements.
 ²³ The idle connection gauge dropping to zero and recovering confirms the completion of a failover.
